source_text: Si \'deus\' commune uocabulum factum est uitio erroris humani, quatenus plures dei dicuntur atque creduntur in saeculo, benedictus tamen deus domini nostri Iesu Christi non alius quam creator intellegetur, qui et uniuersa benedixit — habes Genesim — et ab uniuersis benedicitur — habes Danihelem —; proinde si \'pater* potest dici sterilis deus, [nullius magis nomine quam creatoris] misericordiarum tamen pater idem erit, qui misericors et miserator et misericordiae plurimus dictus est. habes apud Ionam cum ipso misericordiae exemplum, quam Niniuitis exorantibus praestitit, facilis et Ezechiae fletibus flecti, et Achab, marito Iezabel, deprecanti sanguinem ignoscere Nabuthae, et Dauid agnoscenti delictum statim indulgens, malens scilicet paenitentiam peccatoris quam mortem, utique ex misericordiae adfectu. si quid tale Marcionis deus edidit uel edixit, agnoscam \'patrem misericordiarum\'. si uero ex eo tempore hunc titulum ei adscribit, quo reuelatus, quasi exinde sit (pater misericordiarum), quo liberare instituit genus humanum, atquin nos et ex eo tempore negamus illum, ex quo dicitur reuelatus. si enim prius constaret eum esse, tunc et adscribi ei posset. accidens enim est quod adscribitur, accidentia autem antecedit ipsius rei ostensio, cui accidunt. non potest igitur aliquid ei adscribere, quem tunc ostendit, cum aliquid ei adscribit; maxime cum iam alterius est quod adscribitur ei, qui prius non sit . ostensus. tanto (enim) magis negabitur esse, quanto per quod adfirmatur esse, eius est, qui iam ostensus est. Sic et \'testamentum nouum\' non alterius erit quam qui illud repromisit, etsi non litterae at eius spiritus - hoc erit nouitas-, (is) denique, qui litteram tabulis lapideis inciderat, idem et de spiritu edixerat: effundam de meo spiritu in omnem carnem; et si litter a occidit, spiritus uero uiuificat, eius utrumque est, qui ait: ego occidam et ego uiuificabo, percutiam et sanabo. olim duplicem uim creatoris uindicauimus. et iudicis et boni, littera occidentis per legem et spiritu uiuificantis per euangelium. non possunt duos deos facere quae, etsi diuersa, apud unum recenseri praeuenerunt.
pass_a_gloss: If 'god' has become a common term due to the fault of human error, to the extent that many gods are said and believed in the world, nevertheless the blessed God of our Lord Jesus Christ is understood to be not other than the creator, who both blessed all things — you have Genesis — and is blessed by all things — you have Daniel —; accordingly, if the 'father' can be said to be a sterile god, [with no one's name more than the creator's], nevertheless the same one will be the father of mercies, who is said to be merciful and a mercifier and most full of mercies. You have with Jonah an example of his mercies, which he granted to the Ninevites when they prayed, easily swayed by the tears of Hezekiah, and to Ahab, the husband of Jezebel, forgiving the blood of Naboth when he prayed, and to David, immediately forgiving when he acknowledged his fault, certainly preferring the repentance of the sinner to death, from the affection of mercy. If Marcion's god has produced or promulgated anything of this kind, I will acknowledge the 'father of mercies'. But if, on the other hand, he ascribes this title to him from that time when he was revealed, as if he were from then on the father of mercies, because he undertook to free the human race, then we deny him from that time when he is said to have been revealed. For if it were previously established that he existed, then it could also be ascribed to him. For what is ascribed is an accident, and accidents precede the manifestation of the thing to which they happen, to which they are ascribed. Therefore, nothing can be ascribed to him whom he then shows, when he ascribes something to him; especially since what is ascribed to him already belongs to another, who was previously shown. So much the more will he be denied to exist, insofar as what affirms his existence belongs to him who has already been shown. Thus also the 'new testament' will not be of another than the one who promised it, although not of the letter but of the spirit — this will be the newness —, (he) finally, who inscribed the letter on stone tablets, also promulgated concerning the spirit: I will pour out my spirit on all flesh; and if the letter kills, the spirit gives life, both are his, who says: I will kill and I will give life, I will strike and I will heal. Formerly we vindicated the twofold power of the creator, both of the judge and of the good, the letter killing through the law and the spirit giving life through the gospel. They cannot make two gods out of things which, although diverse, were previously reckoned to one.

pass_b_english: Because the word "god" has become a common term through the fault of human error — to the point that many gods are named and believed in throughout the world — the blessed God of our Lord Jesus Christ is still understood to be none other than the Creator. He both blessed all things (you have Genesis) and is blessed by all things (you have Daniel). So even if "Father" can be said of a sterile god — with no one's name more than the Creator's — the same one will be the Father of Mercies, who is called merciful, a mercifier, and most full of mercies. You have an example of his mercy in Jonah, when he granted it to the Ninevites as they prayed; he was easily swayed by Hezekiah's tears; he forgave Ahab, Jezebel's husband, the blood of Naboth when Ahab pleaded; and he immediately forgave David when David acknowledged his fault. He certainly prefers the sinner's repentance to death, purely from the affection of mercy. If Marcion's god has produced or promulgated anything of this kind, I will acknowledge the "Father of Mercies." But if, on the other hand, he ascribes this title to him from the time he was revealed — as if he became the Father of Mercies from then on, because he undertook to free the human race — then we deny him from that very time when he is said to have been revealed. For if his existence had been previously established, then the title could also be ascribed to him. An ascription is an accident, and accidents presuppose the manifestation of the thing to which they belong. Therefore nothing can be ascribed to him whom he then shows, when he ascribes something to him; especially since what is ascribed to him already belongs to another who was previously shown. So much the more will he be denied to exist, because the very thing used to affirm his existence belongs to the one who has already been shown. Thus the "new testament" will not belong to another than the one who promised it, even though it is not of the letter but of the Spirit — this will be the newness. Finally, the one who inscribed the letter on stone tablets also promulgated the promise of the Spirit: "I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh"; and "if the letter kills, the Spirit gives life" — both are his, who says: "I kill and I make alive, I wound and I heal." Formerly we vindicated the twofold power of the Creator: both as Judge and as Good, the letter killing through the Law and the Spirit giving life through the Gospel. They cannot make two gods out of things which, although diverse, were previously reckoned to one.
